parsed.canonical_question: How does the electron transport chain generate reactive oxygen species?

rendering.title: Reactive oxygen species from the transport chain
rendering.body:
The electron transport chain can accidentally produce harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS), mainly at Complexes I and III.

Normally, electrons travel along the chain from NADH or FADH2 all the way to Complex IV, where they reduce oxygen to water. But occasionally an electron escapes this orderly path and reacts directly with an oxygen molecule. Because the electron is transferred one at a time rather than four at once, it produces superoxide (O2•-) — a highly reactive radical.

Complex I is a major source because its flavin group can leak electrons to oxygen under certain conditions, especially when NADH is abundant and the chain is saturated. Complex III can also leak electrons during the Q-cycle, when the unstable ubisemiquinone intermediate passes an electron to oxygen.

Cells manage this by using antioxidant enzymes:
- Superoxide dismutase (SOD) converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
- Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then convert H2O2 to water.

If ROS production overwhelms these defences — a state called oxidative stress — the radicals can damage DNA, proteins, and membrane lipids. This is why mitochondrial ROS are studied in the context of ageing and diseases such as neurodegeneration and cancer.
rendering.summary: Electrons occasionally leak from Complexes I and III to oxygen, forming superoxide. Cells use antioxidant enzymes to neutralise these radicals.
